classification.difficultyReason: Connect irrational roots with the absence of rational intercepts, while explaining positive and negative function values.

content.prompt: Explain why, if we only used rational numbers when drawing graphs in the coordinate plane, the graph of $y=x^2-2$ would lie above and below the $x$-axis, but never intersect it.

answer.short: At $x=0$, $y=-2<0$; at $x=2$, $y=2>0$. Intersections with the $x$-axis require $x=\pm\sqrt{2}$, both irrational, so neither intersection is included when only rational coordinates are used.
answer.worked:
Rational coordinates give points on both sides of the $x$-axis: at $x=0$, $y=-2$, while at $x=2$, $y=2$.

At an intersection with the $x$-axis, $y=0$, so
$$\begin{align*}x^2-2&=0\\x^2&=2\\x&=\pm\sqrt{2}.\end{align*}$$
Both values are irrational. Therefore there is no intersection with rational coordinates, although rational points lie above and below the $x$-axis.
